title: On Hongshi
speaker: Shinmon Michael Newton
summary: Shinmon Michael Newton encourages listeners to approach their experiences with a sense of care and attention, rather than judgment or resistance, by looking at afflictive states like anger and sadness not as obstacles to be overcome, but as opportunities for transformation and growth. This involves cultivating a sense of openness and awareness that allows us to penetrate through conditioning and simply be present with whatever arises, without attachment or aversion. By doing so, we can come to see life and death in their true nature and respond to the world with compassion and clarity.

Look closely.

See for yourself.

How are you doing?
Pretty good?
Yeah?
Oh good.

Great.
Well, I hope as we progress you'll have a little more tranquility, insight, and may you receive whatever your intention is.

I often wondered how those warm-up acts felt, like for the Grateful Dead or Pink Floyd or something like that.
Now I know.
When we talked with Norman he said he's going to talk about koans from the collection that's called in Japanese the Shoyoroku, which Tim yesterday gave us a little taste of.

Now I don't know if everyone here is familiar with koans, so I thought I'd just say a word or two about them, and then to warm you up towards the Shoyoroku I'll talk a little bit about the person who compiled them, Hongzhi.
I'll get to him in just a moment.
But koans are a really bizarre form of literature.
They consist of short dialogues, as the one that Tim read us yesterday, between a Zen teacher and a student.

Sometimes though they're just simply a statement that is given by a Zen teacher, sometimes even just a brief passage from a sutra or one of the Buddhist texts, and sometimes they're just an adage, an off-the-cuff remark that a teacher makes.
At first glance these koans and their commentaries, these commentaries are written often by later Zen teachers, seem quite confusing and even paradoxical.
But koans can give us a very deep insight into the confusing and paradoxical nature of our lives.
Because really, aren't your lives confusing at times and paradoxical, right?
How can you be angry at somebody when you love them so much, for example.
So Norman's going to select some koans from this particular collection, the Shoyoroku, and he'll discuss them in the coming days.
In English the Shoyoroku has been translated two different ways.
Sometimes it's called the Book of Serenity and sometimes the Book of Equanimity.
It depends who the translator is.
So let me now introduce Hongzhi Zhengjue, who is the Chinese ancestor who compiled these koans.
Ancestors, it's another term that came up yesterday.

In Zen temples in Japan and here too in larger Zen centers, we chant this long list of male ancestors, the lineage, which as we all know now is not really a lineage at all, but we chant it at those large centers daily.
If you go to San Francisco Zen Center for example or someplace like that, they'll chant it there.

And recently we've also created a lineage, or not exactly a lineage, but a list of women ancestors, female ancestors, and often that's chanted on alternate days to give a sense of balance, and of course honoring all of the women teachers and ancestors whose names have not been chanted daily at the Zen centers and temples in Asia.

This ritual chanting of names, which to us may seem a little bit strange, comes from the Asian tradition of paying respect to our ancestors, acknowledging the deep debt of gratitude for all of those who lived and came before and laid the foundation for us.
I think we in the West often forget how much we owe to those who came before us.
These days we are all DIYers, right?
Do-it-yourselfers.
Just go to Home Depot, right?
It's written everywhere: do it yourself.
Or perhaps more accurately we are IDIMers.
I did it myself.
But when I stop and consider what I have really accomplished on my own, I really can't come up with much.
After all, just consider, who taught you how to use and hold a spoon, fork and knife?
Who taught you to pet an animal gently, to write a thank-you letter, to read, to sew, to bake bread, to make music, to swim, to wrap a gift, or to meditate?
And who taught them, all of those people who taught you those things?
Most of the things we learn, most of the important things we learn in our life, come from warm hand to warm hand, perhaps with a little help from books or from YouTube these days.
We all have an infinite web of ancestors stretching back through time.
Some are blood ancestors, of course, but most are not.
And yet we are deeply connected to them.
As I said, when I reflect back on my life, very little of my knowledge and skills were really acquired through my own means.
I stand on the shoulders of others.
And in our practice, we stand on the shoulders of our Zen ancestors.
We benefit from their lives, from their teachings, and from their vows.
The strong and grounded commitment of our ancestors to their practice and to later generations is what touches us today.
They vowed, as we do, to end all suffering, to liberate all beings, and to enter all Dharma gates.
Is not our practice the actualization of their vows?
If your suffering and pain has been eased somewhat through this practice, through this way of seeing the world, then the vows of our Zen ancestors have been effective.
And what can we feel but gratitude?
And perhaps the desire to make our intention for our own vows to be carried forward for the sake of our Dharma children and grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
So among those many ancestors was one named Hongzhi Zhengjue.
What kind of teachings did he leave us?
Let me tell you a little bit about Hongzhi first, and then I'll read a few pieces of him.
Hongzhi was born in 1091, and according to the records, he was recognized quite early as a gifted child.
Like all male children in well-off families in China at that time, he studied the Confucian classics.

But his father practiced Zen under a fairly well-known teacher at that time, and this Zen teacher one day noticed Hongzhi and told his father that Hongzhi would be a great Dharma vessel one day, if Hongzhi ordained.
Now whether this is true or part of a story, we don't really know.
But we do know that at age 12 Hongzhi left home and ordained, and he practiced with several well-known Chinese Zen masters at the time.
And at the ripe old age of 21, he had a very strong awakening when he heard some monks chanting a line from the Flower Ornament Sutra, or the Avatamsaka Sutra.
Then according to the records, he kept on practicing and learned from a number of different teachers.
One of those teachers was the famous Chinese teacher who compiled the Blue Cliff Record, which is another collection of koans.
I think those old Chinese Zen guys, they kept collecting these koans.
There are all these books of koan collections, kind of like stamps, I guess.
Get your own book of koans out.
So Hongzhi also compiled his own collection of koans, and one of these collections became the foundation for the Book of Serenity or the Book of Equanimity.
When he was 38 years old, he was asked to teach at a very small and rather dilapidated temple on Mount Taitung.
Once he established himself at that temple, it really flourished.
He was a very well-respected teacher, a very popular teacher.
And it's said he did not leave the mountain for 30 years.
He stayed there, refusing many invitations to teach, until he neared his death.
Then he finally left the mountain to thank his patrons, all the people who had supported the temple through the years that he was teacher there.
Now what's interesting about this?

Although Hongzhi is not directly connected to Dogen, who's the person who went to Japan and brought back this particular school of Zen that we practice today, Hongzhi was Dogen's great Dharma grandfather, so to speak, because Dogen studied at that very temple with his teacher Rujing.
So there's a very interesting connection there.
Now there are a number of stories about Hongzhi that I could tell you, but I just want to tell you one so you get a little flavor of who he was before we go on to his readings.
Before he settled on Mount Taitung, he went to visit a Dharma brother who was assuming this abbacy of a very large monastery.
It was a long trip, but he made this trip on foot, walking across the mountains until he got there, approaching this grand temple.
The attendants there noticed his approach, knowing that he was expected, he was a great friend of the monk who was about to become abbot.
They saw that his clothes and his sandals were quite shabby, ragged and worn.
So quickly, before Hongzhi arrived at the temple gates, they scrambled and found a new pair of sandals for him, straw sandals that they wore in those days.
And when he arrived, they welcomed him and they presented these straw sandals as a gift.
And Hongzhi, taking them, said, "What, did I come here for shoes?"
Let's listen to Hongzhi's words.
Not a lot has been translated of Hongzhi, and I relied partly on this book by Taigen Dan Leighton.
It's called *Cultivating the Empty Field*.
If you just scan this book even briefly, you'll see that these delightful short essays are very lyrical.
He wrote very elegantly on meditation practice and on the meditation experience from the Soto perspective.
So what advice does old man Hongzhi give us for the practice of sitting?
Let's see here.
Hongzhi writes:
*You must completely withdraw from the invisible pounding and weaving of your ingrained ideas.
If you want to be rid of this invisible turmoil, you must just sit through it and let go of everything.
Stay with that just as that.
Stay with this just as this.*
Hongzhi tells us, don't get entangled in stages or goals or judgments, just be fully present with what arises.
One more passage and then I'll read it out.
It's a little bit longer, about a paragraph long, and then we'll examine it in little bits and pieces and see if it's helpful or not.
Hongzhi writes:
*Silently dwell in the self, in true suchness, abandoned conditioning, open-minded and bright without defilement, simply penetrate and drop off everything.
Today is not your first arrival here.
Since the ancient home before the empty kalpa, clearly nothing has been obscured.
Although you are inherently spirited and splendid, still you must go ahead and enact it.
When doing so, immediately display every atom without hiding a speck of dirt.
Dry and cool and deep repose profoundly understand.
If your rest is not satisfying and you yearn to go beyond birth and death, there can be no such place.
Just burst through and you will discern without thought dusts, pure without reasons for anxiety.
Stepping back with open hands is thoroughly comprehending life and death.
Immediately you can sparkle and respond to the world.
Merging together with all things everywhere is just right.*
Pretty dense, eh?
This is how most of the old Zen writings are.
Very dense.
But let's pick it apart a little bit and see if there's something that can be helpful for us.
*Silently dwell in the self.
In true suchness, abandon conditioning, open-minded and bright without defilement.
Simply penetrate and drop off everything.*
Perhaps this brings to mind Dogen's famous phrase regarding the very essence of our zazen practice, Shinjin Datsuraku, or dropping off body and mind.
Hongzhi asks us to silently dwell in the self.
But clearly this is not our daily self that begins to plan and judge as soon as we wake up in the morning.
It's the one that's pushed and pulled around throughout the day by endless streams of thoughts and feelings.
It's not that self.
The self that Hongzhi speaks of here is the one that we become aware of when the chatter begins to quiet a little.
It is the self described in the poem that Tim read for us yesterday.
It is the self we become aware of when we sit.
*Open-minded and bright without defilement.
Simply penetrate and drop off everything.*
So taking our upright posture, allowing the mind and heart to settle by carefully following the breath, by returning to the body, we don't engage with whatever arises.
We don't get entangled with whatever arises.
In this way we put down what Hongzhi calls defilements, that entanglement.
Just put it down and we drop off everything.
I like that expression, to drop off.
It evokes for me the image of a hand that's just gently opening and releasing what we've been grasping onto.
Hongzhi clarifies this a little bit more when he says in a different place:
*Contemplating your own authentic form is how to contemplate Buddha.
Contemplating your own authentic form is how to contemplate Buddha.*
In our zazen practice we contemplate our own authentic form.
We continuously bring our awareness to just as we are at this moment.
Not making judgments, not chasing after our thoughts, not lost in daydreams.
We experience ourselves without distraction.
We experience Buddha, because where else could Buddha be but right here on your cushion?
Drop off everything, Hongzhi tells us.
But this is not easy, as you know.
But it is the way of all Buddhas and all minds who wish to walk the way of the Buddhas.
It is only in this moment that we can really fully sense, inhabit our uprightness.
*So silently dwell in the self.
In suchness, abandon conditioning.
Open-minded and bright without defilement.
Simply penetrate and drop off everything.*
*Today is not your first arrival here.
Since the ancient home before the empty kalpa, clearly nothing has been obscured.*
Today is not your first arrival here.
We all know this in some way.
Maybe as children.
Maybe when we walked in nature, maybe when we listened to music, maybe when our life caused us just to pause for a moment in the midst of our busyness.
At some point we've been touched by a vast openness, free of fear, a spaciousness of heart.
Today is not your first arrival here.
Hongzhi tells us we have been here before.
Indeed we have never left.
It is our ancient home and has been from the beginning of time.
The home that is shining, bright and clear.
This is not a place that we make.
It's not a place that we must get to.
It's not a place that's outside.
It is the most intimate place.
*Since the ancient home before the empty kalpa, clearly nothing has been obscured.
Although you are inherently spirited and splendid, still you must go ahead and enact it.
When doing so, immediately display every atom without hiding a speck of dirt.*
So home, and yet Hongzhi tells us although we are inherently spirited and splendid.
Did you know that about yourself?
You're splendid.
Spirited.
Although this vast openness is our home, still we must go ahead and enact it.
And how do we enact it?
What's Hongzhi telling us here?
Well, our practice is not one of developing anything special like powers and abilities, nor is it gaining anything from the outside like forgiveness or blessings.
And it's not that those things are in some way bad, but they're not our practice.
Our practice is the subtle letting go over and over again of our busyness.
Turning awareness inward and resting clear in this moment.
In this way we enact, we activate, we wake up.

However, this is not a passive process of quieting the mind or turning off the mind, and nor is it certainly a rejection of our bad aspects, because Hongzhi himself admonished us to immediately display every atom without hiding a speck of dirt.
Don't hide it.
Shine your light of awareness on it.
Don't turn away from what arises in our body or mind or our heart, and we don't engage it.
We don't weave story after story or beat ourselves up over it.
In our practice we just shine the light of awareness on it.
So Hongzhi continues.
Let's finish up this last a little bit here.
*Cool and dry in deep repose profoundly understand.
Cool and dry in deep repose profoundly understand.*
Letting go of our judgments and criticisms we come to see our life for what it is.
A moment of sadness, a moment of confusion, a moment of lust, a moment of despair, a moment of sweetness.
We don't hide one speck of dirt.
Even our deepest desires, a desire for awakening, even that we must let go.
Hongzhi writes:
*If your rest is not satisfying and you yearn to go beyond birth and death, there can be no such place.*
Here is the hard nut of our practice.
The very desire of what we want most is what obscures.
At some point even that must be let go.
Then:
*Stepping back with open hands is thoroughly comprehending life and death.
Immediately you can sparkle and respond to the world.
Merge together with all things.
Everywhere is just right.*
What would that be like, eh?
I'm Canadian so I say eh a lot.
What would that be like, to live where everywhere is just right?
Just right.
Here in the zendo, body getting a bit achy.
Just right.
Lonely at home or away on business and a bit sad.
It's just right.
Helping a sick one is just right.
Hands open.
Hands open.
We offer our life.
Everywhere we sparkle and respond to the world, fulfilling our bodhisattva vows.
When I read this line I immediately thought of Anna Grace.
Anna Grace is a member of our sangha.
And there was one period where everything she had to put sparkles on.
You know the glue, those gluey sparkles you buy.
In fact we've got it on our kitchen still I think, and at the zendo there's still sparkle on the floor.
I thought, Anna Grace sparkles, and she spread it around.
Everywhere we sparkle and respond to the world, fulfilling our bodhisattva vows.
Sometimes the beginning of sesshin, the first day or two, is pretty challenging for us.
We become aware of our mind and see it's like a rushing stream after a heavy rain, full of thoughts, memories, plans, admonishments.
Our mind seems to rush this way and that.
We see our mind as it is through much of our daily activity.
Then, and I hope maybe you've tasted this already, we begin to settle.

We settle our awareness on our breath, on our body, just gently returning to them over and over again, with our only intention, our only intention being not to follow the many threads that our mind presents to us.
But still, that's no time to doze.
Hongzhi calls to us to illuminate the source, to enter that vast, bright and empty field.

Bringing over and over again our full and careful attention to our body, our present experience, perhaps with a sense of wordless curiosity, we come to illuminate that bright field of emptiness, continuing to drop our judgments about others, about ourselves, about what we need to do or should have done.
We take the backward step into the field of light.
So I hope you have found the words of our ancestor Hongzhi helpful.
But if they're confusing or if you simply doze off for most of this talk, that's fine.
Just let those words go, but listen.
Listen to the watery cry of the eagles.
Listen to the primeval croaking of the heron as it flies overhead.
Listen to the early morning chorus of the robins and the soft snapping beaks of the swallows as they glide around your legs picking up little insects that you have stirred up from the grass.
Listen to them.
They are all saying the same thing.
They are all saying the same thing.
